If you play Jyhad as per its design, which includes access to and use of
arbitrary numbers of cards. If you throw in extraneous restriction,
that's no longer necessarily true, as demonstrated by the Malk deck
winning Gencon.

>This balance is due in large part to the number of
>"built in duplicates", or varied cards that have roughly the same
>effect. There are many different cards that give stealth, or intercept,
>or whatever.

Your whatever list would be very short. The only others are Fortitude
prevent damage and Dominate +bleed. Incidentally, you'll note that the
need for multiple stealth and intercept comes from the fact that you can
only use one of each modifier per action. So to make +5 stealth possible,
you need 5 different stealth cards.

>Those effects that can be achieved by only one specific
>card are rarely needed more than three or four times in any game.

BWAANH!!! Next contestant, please?
There are many, many, unduplicated (and inadequately substitutable) cards
DESPERATELY needed in quantity:

Bewitching Oration: Try a non-prince vote deck without lots of these.
Dodge: Ever wonder how people can survive the Gangrel without Fortitude?
Telepathic Counter: Essential bleed defense for most Auspex decks.
Deflection: Essential bleed defense for most Dominate decks.
Dread Gaze: Essential vote defense for many Presence decks.
Theft of Vitae: Unless your Tremere bring magazines to read for the first
round :-)
Flash: The only good way for Celerity to maneuver
Movement of the mind: Essential for Tremere maneuver defenses.
Fake Out: Essential for Nosferatu and Ally maneuver defenses.
Form of the Ghost: Essential for Gangrel fighting guns.
Computer Hacking: Essential for weenie bleed decks.
Majesty: Essential for escaping combat with a multi-clan Presence deck.
Camarilla Exemplary/Conservative Agitation: The core of almost any vote
deck. Between the 2, you need 12-20 or the vote deck can't win.
Camarilla Exemplary: Yes, there are ways to bleed besides stealth.
Aching Beauty: A particularly nice version for Toreador.
Cats' Guidance: Animalism defense.
Cloak the Gathering: The only way to pass around stealth.
Thrown Sewer Lid/ Thrown Gate. Yeah, sure you can run a pitch deck with
only 6 strike cards.
Boxed In/Dead End Alley: How do you think the Tremere get to the second
round?
Bum's Rush: The critical card for non-intercept combat decks.
etc. (and this DOES go on, for a long time)

You'll note that almost all of these cards are common. The fact that good
decks work from stacks of common cards (and not $$$ rare substitutes) is
the reason you don't need $$$ to play Jyhad (even in a roomful of Mr.
Suitcases), which is one of it's great elements.

>Each skill is strong inone aspect of the game, and weak in others. To
>play protean for stealth (with a deck full of Earth Controls) is to
>play protean ineffectively.

Not necessarily. That would be an exotic use, but I imagine there's
something to be done with it, and I'd like to see it. (Hmm.
Gangrel/Ventrue Seductive Bleed - hey, you may have something there!
Isn't it great to play a game where even relatively exotic concepts can
make workable decks?)

>If my deck features the dominate skill, I
>have many cards that can modify my bleed, and I shouldn't need more than
>four of any one of them.

Yes, you can bleed adequately with Dominate (albeit with a very boring and
predictable cardset). But when all bleed decks must have Dominate, the
game gets pretty stereotyped. A great joy of Jyhad is that almost every
clan or basic clan combination can bleed, vote, OR fight, and EVERY clan
or clan combination can defend itself against all three strategies. Hence
you don't see much of the Magic phenomena "Oh, you're playing a weenie
deck. I don't have a chance against that".

>Every skill has been given its fair share of
>these "built in duplicates", and playing WITHOUT limits DEFEATS the
>balance that is so fundamentally a part of Jyhad's design.

Really? What are the Presence and Animalism duplicates?

>A four card limit is not a problem. When the balance that
>is part of Jyhad has been established, so many more options for style
>of play will be open to you, and each will have an equal chance of
>succeeding. Your games will become more interesting. You will build
>decks you never dared before. You will have more FUN.

Jyhad has three basic strategies - bleed, combat, and vote. Since bleed
doesn't require cards but the others do, with tight card limits, bleed
becomes the only strategy. Likewise, of the three bleed tactics, Stealth
and Tap require cards, so only Bruise, with combat equipment (read guns,
read slow) remains. While my group had 4-card limits, we were eventually
forced to bar Malk decks (they always won, unless the whole table ganged
up), and that's exactly what the game degenerated into - lots of slow
Bruise and Bleed decks.

By contrast, without limits, the game explodes into a kaleidoscopic
variety of strategies and tactics. In my Strategies and Clans article I
outlined 20 fundamentally different decks (none required lots of rares,
natch). There are many more; I guesstimate just under 100 fundamentally
different decks. Games go faster without limits, too.

In terms of fun, you haven't played CCGs until you've played CCGs without
card limits. Card limits detract so from deckbuilding, deck tweaking, and
(in Jyhad) strategy that even games that are broken without limits (Magic)
are still a hoot played without limits. When the game works without
limits, you really get to see the real fun of a CCG - trading, playing,
and deckbuilding, all extensively, in a varied and ever-changing
environment.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Guess what. I play with a THREE card limit...

...and I have fun every time.

Unlike any other card game, Jyhad has a balance between its many facets
built right into the cards themselves. Each discipline, clan, etc, has

its function, and when properly played, is niether more nor less power-

ful than any other. This balance is due in large part to the number of

"built in duplicates", or varied cards that have roughly the same
effect. There are many different cards that give stealth, or intercept,

or whatever. Those effects that can be achieved by only one specific

card are rarely needed more than three or four times in any game.

Each skill is strong inone aspect of the game, and weak in others. To

play protean for stealth (with a deck full of Earth Controls) is to

play protean ineffectively. If my deck features the dominate skill, I

have many cards that can modify my bleed, and I shouldn't need more than

four of any one of them. Every skill has been given its fair share of

these "built in duplicates", and playing WITHOUT limits DEFEATS the
balance that is so fundamentally a part of Jyhad's design.

Trust me. A four card limit is not a problem. When the balance that

is part of Jyhad has been established, so many more options for style
of play will be open to you, and each will have an equal chance of
succeeding. Your games will become more interesting. You will build
decks you never dared before. You will have more FUN.

-p.

Theme and concept decks can be very interesting and fun, and many cannot
operate in a wild environment. However, 4-card doesn't reduce power
enoughfor theme decks, it just shuts down any deck with a reliance on a
small set of cards. I actually find that theme and concept decks end up
drawing from a small set of cards, comparable to that of a 2-clan
1-discipline deck, and card limits are particularly painful to exactly
that kind of deck.

If I want serious theme decks, I find it necessary to play under
"gentlevampire's agreement" to not play typical tuned decks. Restrictions
like 4-card produce Jyhad variants, which can be interesting, but I prefer
to change such restrictions frequently as most variants I've seen have
optimal strategies which pop up after a few playings, making the variant,
well, not very varied.

My decks all have strong personalities and could usually be considered
thematic. I consider it part of the pleasure to build theme decks that
are also functioning play decks, and greatly enjoy my "Feeling a little
Under the Weather" deck which is basically Tremere skulking about poising
the blood supply, my Visionaries deck leading the Camarilla to freedom
form the Methuseleh (except me, of course :-) or my Things that go Bump in
the Night deck (which plays like it's made of a group of terrorists).
These theme decks tend to demand large numbers of particular cards even
more than my more powerful decks, which rarely use more than 8 of any
card.

the more creative a player must be, and the more enjoyable the game becomes.

wish (eighty seems to be about optimal) but the 5 card limit still applies.

You're mixing enter combat resources with fight combat resources. All the
presses and undead strengths in the world will do you no good if you can't
get into a fight. Indeed, they will jam your hand, causing a couple of
rounds of inactivity as you clear then out with your 1 per turn discard.
Permanent intercept alone won't save you from a Malk predator - it takes
too long to get out. If you're not his initial prey, and you manage to
get some out, your survival will depend on the timing of his Seduction
cards. (Do people really enjoy having games determined by predictable
luck issues?) BTW, without card limits Animalism becomes an intercept
discipline which CAN adequately back a permanent-driven interception
strategy, a typical example of the expansion of strategies from playing
without card limits.

Your only enter combat resources are 4 Bum's Rushes and 4 Havens. 1 Malk
can still oust you, so you have to torporize at least 4 Malks. That
requires, on average, that you go through half your deck in just a few
turns (because that's all you'll have). Even real Jyhad decks, built fast
and coherent, can't really manage that. Slow, permanent-heavy, 4-card
decks don't have a chance. In addition, the Malk will sometimes survive
the combat (with guns), Sudden a Haven Uncovered or simply pull some guys
out of torpor. This will correspondly increase the need for enter combat.

Even if your opponents lack rush defense, you need at least 12 rush cards
for a reliable enter combat ability. If they have rush defense, you'll
need more.

>Go with the card limits! They make for interesting games.

If you consider slow, luck-driven games in which decks are forced to
minimalize personality "interesting", sure. But for that sort of game,
War is cheaper. :-)

Well, since this has gone on for quit a while now, I hope you'll
forgive me as I save myself some keystrokes:

The short answer is: Unique cards, restrictions on playability of cards.
(Action Mods/Reactions/Giant's Blood/Parity Shift/etc.)

Curt (as usual) has thought this thing out far more than most, so here's
his POV:

From: curt...@aol.com (CurtAdams)
Newsgroups: rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad
Subject: Re: Card Restrictions
Date: 7 Jun 1995 22:24:56 -0400
Message-ID: <3r5n1o$6...@newsbf02.news.aol.com>

Jyhad is not Magic. In Magic you have multiple cards to permit
functioning under card limits. In Jyhad, you have multiple + intercept
and + stealth cards because you can only use one of each and they WOULD
like it to be possible to get intercept or stealth above 1. Under card
limits, this has the decidedly peculiar side effect of permitting
intercept and stealth decks while the other fascinating uses of those
disciplines get hosed.

Magic was originally designed with the assumption that people would play
in "universes" of less than 2000 cards. After all, what kind of nut case
would spend hundreds of dollars to win a card game? Hence Magic was
designed with the assumption that players would face loose card limits -
not exactly 4, but unlimited numbers just wouldn't be available. When it
became clear that some people would pay thousands to win, and have access
to more or less unlimited numbers of any card, they slapped on a 4-card
limit in a desperate attempt to simulate the limits they had expected. It
took a lot of the flavor out, but they had to do something. It really
didn't fix things, even - look at the length of the restricted list!
Since about Arabian Nights, WotC has been trying to eliminate the need for
card limits so the game can be played as intended. They haven't
succeeded, but at least they are trying.

By the time of the design of Jyhad, WotC KNEW that people were going to
have lots of the cards. Jyhad was designed on the principle that people
were going to have access to unlimited commons, and perhaps to unlimited
uncommon and rares too. For Jyhad to work, you MUST have unlimited
numbers of many essential cards - Bum's Rush, Deflections, Dodge, Undead
Strength, Flash, Fake Out, Telepathic Counter, etc. Otherwise the
defense/offense, vote/combat/bleed, and clan balances go poof. Yes, there
are some problem cards, like Wake, 5th Tradition, and Majesty (which
actually is one of the cards you need in quantity), but those have to be
addressed on an individual basis. You don't fix a few problem cards by
wrecking the whole game structire.

The great tragedy of WotC's earlier mistake with Magic is this 4-card
business. It would be excessive to punish WotC for that one mistake,
especially given that they recognized it promptly and are trying to fix
it. But that mistake is being used to punish the entire CCG industry.
Every game that comes out, people want to put 4-card limits on - whether
the limits are inadequate (Rage), irrelevant (INWO), or downright
destructive (Jyhad). Almost every game is getting stuck with all the
pains of card limits - differing effects on different cards, the tedium of
card counting to ensure legality, the mindlessness of throwing in 4 of
each necessary card, etc. After playing a good no-limits-needed game,
believe me, card limits will drive you NUTS.

In CCGs, as in underwear, one size does NOT fit all.
-----
[Continuity break imposed by LSJ]
-----
(Peter Gordon WILSMORE) writes:

>Limiting cards is a really good idea otherwise you can get real nasty
(and
>impossible to stop) malkavian bleed decks (bleed, stealth, slealth,
bleed,
>stealth, slealth, bleed, stealth, slealth, bleed, stealth, slealth).

You think 4 card is a problem for the Malkavians? Well, let's see what
that actually does to the Malks:

Sneak Cards:
4 Cloak the Gathering
4 Faceless Night
4 Lost in Crowds
4 Mask of 1000 Faces
4 Seduction
4 Spying Mission
4 Psychic Veil

Bleed Cards
4 Bonding
4 Conditioning
4 Deflection
4 Computer Hacking
4 Govern the Unaligned
4 Kine Dominance
4 Threats
1 Pulse of the Canaille

4 Guns, 11 Masters

80 Cards total.

Now, assuming each Veil gets used for 1 bleed and the Pulse gets used
twice, he can get 58 points of bleed at a total of +36 Stealth, with 4
Seductions for that extra boost and 4 Deflections for some delightful
little surprises. *Such* a hardship. (Of course, if he hasn't got $$$, he
probably doesn't have 4 PV and 4 KD, but hey, why should we let people
without $$$ have a shot at the big leagues by allowing them to use extras
of the roughly equivalent Lost in Crowds plus Govern the Unaligned?) Mr.
Malk can still easily clear the table, but at least you have the
consolation of knowing that due to card limits, his deck has become
completely, utterly predictable, with no options left for variety within
the context of stealthy bleeds.

Now let's look at what 4-card limits do to DEFENSES against our friendly
neighborhood Malk. There are 3 main defenses against stealthy bleed:
intercept, rush, and bounce. Now the interceptors don't really care about
card limits any more than the Malks do, as there are umpty-umph +
intercept cards. Tremere and combat Malkavians do just fine. Toreador
theoretically could, except with all that intercept about they can't get
out any guns and they no longer have any good way to hurt people.

Now the bouncers (people using Deflection/ Telepathic Misdirection to
bounce bleeds to their prey) used to cackle madly at the prospect of a
Malkavian predator, who they just used to oust their prey. Hearing that
Mr. Malk was building an "unbeatable" deck by cranking up the proportion
of Conditionings merely increased the volume on their cackle. Nothing
like your predator spending extra blood to bleed YOUR prey.

Once again, the Malks and the Tremere are sitting pretty. Granted, with
only 4 of each they no longer COMPLETELY hose the Sneak and Bleed decks,
but they have intercept too, so they're still smiling.

Mr. Ventrue, however, can only bounce 4 bleeds (no telepathics for HIM).
His cackle dies in his throat. Quick, can he find another defense?
Intercept - sorry, no intercept in his disciplines. Rush - sorry again,
Fortitude is pretty lousy at doing damage. He's now helpless.
Congratulation, card limits have claimed their first victim, as Ventrue
degenerates from an outstanding anti-Malk deck to a very low speed bump.

Toreador bleed bouncers get hosed too. Their remaining bounce card
(Telepathic Misdirection) isn't even as good as Deflection, and the poor
man's bleed bounce (Telepathic Counter) doesn't do much good when you can
only have 4. They, too, have become speed bumps. At least they are high
speed bumps as the combination of Auspicious intercept and Celeritous
Dodges allows them to survive a long time.

What about rushers? Rush is based on the principle that the best defense
is a good offense. In rush, you play a combat god deck, with lots of
cards for entering combat (Bum's Rush, Haven Uncovered, etc.) Typically a
nasty Brujah rush doesn't care how many Bleed or Stealth cards a Malk
predator has because he sends the Malks to torpor as fast as they get
influenced out.

Under 4-card, though, things change. With only 4 Bum's Rush and 4 Haven,
Mr. Brujah can only get into combat 8 times (and the Havens can be
Suddened). At most, he can get 2 players. Typically, he can't even get
one, because with only 8 enter combat cards he's guaranteed a dry spell
where he can't find an enter combat card and he's just going to get mowed
down. It will only take one surviving Malk to do the job. Victim #3.

Nosferatu and Gangrel lose rush for similar reasons. They have access to
raven spies, at least, so if they are very lucky they will a) not start
with a Malk predator, b) draw and play multiple Ravens and Sports Bikes,
c) not get their one +2 interceptor socked with a Seduction and d) manage
to have the right cards in hand to torporize multiple Malkavians. Not as
long a shot as winning the lottery, but, still, 9 times out of 10, <thump>
<thump>
- more speed bumps.

So what do we have? Malkavian stealthy bleed decks are reduced from being
able to clear the table to - being able to clear the table slightly more
slowly. Sniff. Meanwhile, 5 out of the 7 clans lose the (otherwise VERY
effective) defenses against Malkavian stealth and bleed. Jeez, what more
would they want?

than leaving the cards unfixed and unlimited - and certainly far better
than blanket limits.

A point system will create a $$$ barrier of sorts - most decks will
increase in power as the number of "point" cards in them go up. Hence you

I have not played in a Jyhad tournament ever, so anything I have to say
will come from Theoretical and not Practical experience. That said:, I
have two caveats about point systems:

1) The problem cards would never get fixed/removed/errataedin any future
printings, because they have been 'fixed for tournaments' - and that's all
that really counts, no?
2) If there were a point system, it might (only might) dissuade designers
from continuing their so-far excellent job of balancing the cards. If an
unbalanced/unbalancing card can simpoly be given a (higher) point-value,
then it might be seen as a lesser evil than if the object is to create a
no-limits _ever_ card game...

: While I think most of us agree that card limits

: are a bad thing (or at least, 4-card limits are bad),

Yup. Yup. uh-huh.

: most of us also agree

: that there are certain problem cards in a limitless environment.

The salient point here is that almost everyone agrees on _what_ these
problem cards are, and at least half of them fall into the category of
untap cards.

: Given that

: we are not going to go in and change existing cards to give them a cost,
: or increase their existing cost, does a point system seem a viable option?

Simple question: why is that a given?

Whatever you do, you are going to have to disseminate this information
well in advance to ensure that everyone can properly and legally create
their deck. Also, based on the Magic experience, whatever you _do_ set
down for tournament rules is eventually going to become the de facto
rules for normal house play.

How about this for a solution then: instead of a limited list, or its
equivalent in a point-value system, simply issue a list of the card-fixes
_for tournament purposes only_. This could include things like:

- having WWEF cost 1 blood
- Having Majesty cost 1 blood
- Declaring that Theft of Vitae can only be used once per round
- Stating that a Freak Driven vampire cannot perform the same _category_
of action again this round.

Etc. You know as well as we do what the problem cards are, and probably
know how they should be fixed. (If not, asl: We'll be only too happy to
tell you. :-)

This will have several beneficial effects:

- The judges will not have to look over every single deck to ensure that
they meet the point standards: a long and tiresome process which takes up
much of the judges' and event's time.
- Any sort of limits (and point-values count too) can be gotten around by
cheating should the person be unscrupulous enough to sneak in cards
and put them in after the count.
- It still allows people to build whatever sort of deck they want, and the
other players at the table can be called on to help enforce the Tournament
Errata, as it is in their best interest.
- The Tournament Errata would eventually become (in the manner described above)
unofficially official, and the 'problem cards' would be fixed (of
a sort) without ever having to take them out of print or re-issue them.

I believe this to be at least as valid a solution as the points-value one,
probably with better long-term effects for the game as a whole.

I would love to hear a public response to this idea, even if only to tell
me why it won't work and has already been rejected.

: For example, maybe Majesty is worth 1 point, Freak Drive is worth 2 points,

: WWEF is worth 1 point, and a deck's point total is limited to 20% of the
: number of cards in it.

I have never really tried the Majestic Bleed deck (not having enough
Majesties for it), but isn't 20% Majesty about the right number? And
not like this deck needs anything else that would be on the banned list...
I doubt that this _particular_ point-value would be much of a solution at
all.

I don't think it would work very well.

1) such a system is hard both to build a deck under and to verify that the
players are following the rules.

2) Hard to balance. Look at any game where you can design your own widget, or
build an army from points. Those are balancing nightmares, and only work
after years of playtesting and revisions.

different cards - why tie them together?

An easier solution in the same vein - a "restricted" list of cards that you
couldn't have more than 10% of your deck being. From a game play perspective,
this is not nearly as satisfying as Shane's list of fixes, but fits in with the
way you guys like to balance things.

making all untaps cost one extra blood. Why? Because it changes a rule of the
game that's not obvious, especially to newcomers. My question : how is a way
to limit the number of any particular card in a deck fundamentally different
than this? That's a rule change too. You still need a list of cards and
what's different about them (in this case, the rule change is that you can't
have more than X in your deck).

You guys did a marvelous fix on fame, by adding the word "Unique" to it.

can't do it).

Viola. No need for card limits. No need for extensive lists of what you can

and can't do while building your deck. Infinitely simpler than MtG tourny
rules.

So: two lines of changes (cancelling the errata doesn't count, since that was
extra in the first place), and I challenge my fellow readers to make an
"abusive" deck under those rules.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
ch...@fpah1.dseg.ti.com (Charles T. Schwope) writes:

> I hate to say it, but try to find someone to play non-tourney rules
>with you in MtG. Next to, if not totally, impossible.

The reason this is true in Magic is because the rules that come with the game
aren't play balanced. Players tend to want rules that don't make it obvious
what the best strategy is so they look elsewhere. A number of Magic clubs
or groups make their own deck construction rules but the easiest thing to do
is to use another set of deck construction rules that WotC has blessed and
anointed in some way: Duelist Convocation rules. If the rules in the game
box (well, starter decks in this case) were reasonable, I very much doubt this
would happen. Tournament rules decks would probably be mainly limited to
players that were trying to test them for tourneys.

> If tourney rules are released for VTES, they will become the standard
>to build decks by (most likely).

Um, the DC _DID_ release tourney rules for VTES (basically 60-80 card decks,
no limits) and even WotC didn't use them at Gencon. Blackly humorous in a
way but it does demonstrate my point. Rules get used when there's some
attraction to them. The two main factors affecting which deck construction
rules people use are:

How do they contribute to play-balance? Do they make it difficult to find an
invulnerable strategy? Or do you have to "trust" your opponent not to use an
obvious strategy to have a decent game (when you don't use the same one)?

How universally accepted are they? Who advocates them? Do they come with the
game (best)? Or are they advocated by a respected nationwide or worldwide
organization that advertises or even markets them (second best)? Are they
some "player's standard" that seems "universally" accepted (this doesn't exist
but I would think it would be third best)? Or are they just some rules your
local play group thought up (least useful in this respect)?

(One other factor involves the undesirability of using tournament rules in
informal play, since some of the deck construction rules were conceived for
tournaments for reasons that don't have anything to do with informal play,
mainly time constraints.)

The problem with Magic right now is that these two factors are working against
one another. The most well-known rules are also the worst. On the other hand,
a lot of local play groups probably have great deck construction rules but
such rules are worthless outside of the group. So DC rules win by default.
In Jyhad, DC rules aren't much different then the original rules. On the
other hand, neither the DC nor the original rules address what seems to be
a popular concern with limiting overpowered cards. If what was meant by the
statement that was quoted above was: "If the DC comes out with rules that limit
cards in some way (particularly overpowered ones) everyone will start using
them.", I agree that they may become quite popular. This would be the Magic
situation all over again where DC rules are perceived as better play-balanced
than the game-box rules and thus get used more often. But that would be
unfortunate because, like Magic, the issue of which deck construction players
should use would never get settled. Ugh!

I agree with with the people who say, "Let's just fix the overpowered cards."

Fred

[long diatribe follows]

I signed up for the officially sanctioned VTES tournament at GenCon. From
the time that I signed up until the time that I actually sat down at a
table (after signing in to the tournament), there were no card limits for
deck-building. Note that this includes all of the time that I spent
actually building my deck.

In the following fifteen minutes, WotC introduced its four-card limit.
Why? As an experiment, according to Tom. Now, I don't know how many
of you have tried it, but if you build a deck with a four-card limit,
and a deck without a per-card limit, they will often end up with different
compositions. In fact, the deck you built with no limits may not even
be legal in a limited environment.

But never fear -- participants were given that fifteen minutes to redo
their decks to meet this restriction. So that deck that you spent up
to 3 months building and tuning under the published tournament rules for
this officially sanctioned tournament, you should have no problem tuning
down to some arbitrary set of restrictions chosen purely for experimental
purposes.

Unfortunately, I did not bring any cards other than my built (incorrectly,
surprise, surprise) deck, so I couldn't tweak to meet the new requirements.
There was another player who was generous (I'm being serious here) enough
to offer me some additional commons from his stash if I wanted.

But like I said, I had spent some time thinking about and organizing my
deck in the months before GenCon, and I didn't think 15 minutes of
tearing asunder and rebuilding was going to produce the same level of
effectiveness. So I signed out and got my money back. Of course, now it
was too late to join another game, since the WotC staff didn't actually
get its collective act together until about 15 minutes after starting
time to announce the deck-building restrictions (then giving another
15 minutes after that to tune).

So I would disagree with Tom's assertion. Yes, saying "four-card limit"
instead of "no limit" is not a major rules change, but it is a major
deck-building change. In any tournament, the rules should be announced
ahead of time if they are going to affect a player's preparation for
that event. "Okay decathalon contestants, this Olympics we're going to
replace the high jump with a water ski jump. Just a little change, we
feel like experimenting with the format. Since you've trained so long
on the other events, we'll give you the rest of the day to practice
you skiing, and then run that event tomorrow. Good luck!"

In a sanctioned tournament, the completely standard tournament rules
should be followed. Otherwise, why bother having an official set
of tournament rules in the first place?

All of this is moot for me, of course, as I will not participate in
another WotC-sponsored event. I have had several negative experiences
with WotC convention staff (at other cons as well as GenCon 95) since
they came to power after the release of Magic. It's just not worth it
to me when I can be hanging out with polite game designers who don't
f*ck with their product on a whim. (Note: nobody at GenCon was impolite;
I had that run-in at DragonCon 94).

Hunter

: I suspect that a lot of the Jyhad players who "hate" Magic just burned out

: of the Magic players who "hate" Jyhad dislike the fact that it's generally
: not degenerate :) or just don't like group play. It would probably be
: illuminating to get a sense of what someone with one of those opinions
: thinks about other games in the industry.

Most Magic players I have encountered are not diplomatic, crafty, wily,
strategic, however you choose to describe it, to succeed in a multiplayer
environment. (Cf. an excellent thread on *.magic.misc called "Group Game
Stereotypes.") The harsh environment of the duel has trained them to
obliterate their opponent with little regard to threats from their right or
left; they understand little of politics, of deal-striking, of reneging
on deals, and thus either self-destruct or act ill-advisedly when they try
to play Jyhad.

For example: would you invite someone who only enjoyed kickboxing to play
Diplomacy with you and your friends? I don't think so. Thankfully, there
are those who learn the subtleties of Jyhad -- but they usually give up
Magic soon after.

- Neil

that used to be pumping through some living thing. This is why Hunting Grounds

The problem is not "playing to win" or "making degenerate decks" or such.
The problem is, (mostly) games are played and discussed because of
their mathematical interest - i.e. most games are intractably complex.
A game for which a degenerate, "unbeatable" deck exists arouses little
mathematical interest, because the game can be considered solved.
Such a game is no fun in the first place, not players who build
"degenerate decks" making it no fun.

You don't see tic-tac-toe being discussed in rec.games.abstract,
because the game is solved. You don't see adults playing it too
often, either (except playing with kids, and deliberately making
non-optimal moves so that they lose sometimes). The game is
solved, so induces little further mathematical interest.

Sorry, I'm sometimes overly fond of abbreviations and nicknames.

A Freak Bleed deck consists of (basically) Freak Drive, Majesty, Threats,
and 5th Traditions, wielded by Ventrue Princes and + bleeders (Democritus,
who is both, is ideal).

Every turn a vampire takes actions, he bleeds multiple times, using
Majesty to untap when blocked and Freak Drive when not blocked, pitching
Threats as necessary. When it runs out of blood, it 5th Traditions to get
its blood back. Theoretically, it can clear a table the first turn it
gets actions, although that seems fairly unlikely. It's a gruesomely and
excessively good deck; only fairly specialized anti-Majesty defenses have
a good chance against it.

manipulate Dimple into torching the vermin. He believes he is toasting
